notes.6: There were some candidates who thought that the air resistance is zero when a skydiver is travelling at constant speed. They confused this with zero resultant force.
notes.7: There was some confusion here with candidates not showing an understanding that when an object moves in a circle at constant speed there is a resultant force towards the centre of the circle.
notes.8: Only the better performing candidates answered this correctly and recognised that force = rate of change of momentum.
notes.9: Candidates needed to recognise that the work done against gravity is dependent on the vertical height that the object is moved, not the total distance.
notes.10: The most common error was to use the energy going to heat up the room, rather than the energy used to light the room.
notes.11: This was answered correctly by almost all candidates.
notes.12: Many candidates thought that the atmosphere only supports a shorter column of mercury when the barometer tube is wider.
notes.14: A significant number of candidates thought that energy is absorbed when the mercury solidifies. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics March 2017
notes.15: The majority of candidates thought that neither change would increase the sensitivity of the thermometer. This could be because they did not understand the term ‘sensitivity’ or because they did not appreciate the physics of the situation.
notes.16: The question demonstrated the need for candidates to recognise the correct units. Thermal capacity is defined as the energy needed to cause unit rise the temperature of a body, hence the unit must be J / °C.
notes.17: The question was answered well; a number of candidates thought that electrons carried the current in all liquids.
notes.18: A number of candidates thought that a shiny surface emitted radiation at a greater rate than a dull surface.

notes.23: The question was often answered correctly; a significant minority of candidates thought that sound travels by longitudinal waves.
notes.24: Candidates found this question challenging as they did not recognise the idea that sound is produced by vibrating sources and that ultrasound is very high frequency (greater than 20 kHz).
